criteria.name: Problem 1
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 1 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 1. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
1. Explain why f(m, 1) = 1.
[1 pt.]
1

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
1. Since there is only one student, no muﬃn needs to be cut, so the student receives only
whole muﬃns.

criteria.name: Problem 2
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
2. Compute, with explanation, f(1, s).
[2 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
2. One muﬃn needs to be divided fairly among s students, so each student gets a total of
1/s of a muﬃn. Since the one muﬃn can be divided into s evenly-sized pieces of 1/s
each, no student needs to receive a piece smaller than that. So f(1, s) = 1/s.

criteria.name: Problem 3
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
3. Compute, with explanation f(ks, s) where k is any positive integer.
[2 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
3. By giving each student k uncut muﬃns every student receives their fair share of the
muﬃns and no one needs to receive a piece that is smaller than a whole muﬃn. Thus
f(ks, s) = 1.

criteria.name: Problem 4
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
4. Explain why, if m is not a multiple of s as in the previous problem, f(m, s) ≤1/2.
[2 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
4. To divide m muﬃns fairly among s students, each student receives m/s muﬃns. But
since m is not a multiple of s, the number m/s is not an integer. Thus each student
must receive some fraction of some muﬃn. In other words, at least one muﬃn needs
to be cut into two of more pieces. If any piece of this muﬃn is larger than 1/2 then
the remaining pieces must total less than 1/2 of a muﬃn. Thus, some student must
receive a piece that is less than 1/2 in size. Thus, if any muﬃn must be cut, the best
that could be hoped for is if all muﬃns that must be cut will be divided into two equal
pieces, so that no one receives a piece smaller than 1/2. Thus f(m, s) ≤1/2.

criteria.name: Problem 5
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 1 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 1. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
5. Any way of dividing m muﬃns fairly among s students leads to muﬃn division tables
such as those created by the students to display how they divided 5 muﬃns among
3 students. Explain why the numbers in each column of a muﬃn division table must
add to 1.
[1 pt.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
5. The numbers in a column of a muﬃn division table are the sizes of the pieces into
which any particular muﬃn is cut. Reassembling these pieces gives one whole muﬃn,
so the sum of the numbers in a column of the table is 1.

criteria.name: Problem 6
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
6. Compute, with explanation, the sum of the numbers in any row of a muﬃn division
table.
[2 pts.]
The next few problems will show that f(5, 3) = 5/12. That is, there is no way to cut up
ﬁve muﬃns so that all students can receive 5/3 of a muﬃn and the smallest piece anyone
must receive is larger than 5/12. Since 5 is not a multiple of 3, from problem 4 there must
be at least one piece that is no larger than 1/2 in size. Thus, if any muﬃn in any division
remains uncut (i.e. one student received a whole muﬃn as well as some other pieces) then
instead cut that muﬃn into two pieces of size 1/2 and give both to that student. Since
f(5, 3) ≤1/2 this cut doesn’t change the size of the smallest piece anyone will receive. Thus,
it may be assumed that in the division of the muﬃns that guarantees the largest possible
smallest piece, all muﬃns are cut into at least two pieces.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
6. The numbers in a row of a muﬃn division table are the sizes of the pieces that each
student receives from each muﬃn. The sum of these numbers is thus the total amount
of muﬃn that the student receives. Since the muﬃns are divided fairly, this total must
be a fair share of the muﬃns: m/s.

criteria.name: Problem 7
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
7. Explain why, to make the largest possible smallest piece, no muﬃn should be cut into
more than two pieces.
[2 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
7. If a muﬃn is cut into three or more pieces, at least one of those pieces is 1/3 of a muﬃn
or less. Since the students have already found a division of the muﬃns where everyone
receives no pieces that are smaller than 5/12 and 5/12 > 1/3, the “best” division of
the muﬃns can’t require a muﬃn to be cut into three or more pieces.

criteria.name: Problem 8
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

8. Since, by the previous problem, all muﬃns should be cut into two pieces, there are
ten pieces of muﬃns. Use the pigeon-hole principle to show that someone must have a
piece that is no larger than 5/12.
[2 pts.]
Hence, f(m, s) ≤5/12. Since a method of dividing the muﬃns was found where the
smallest piece was 5/12 this completes the proof that f(5, 3) = 5/12. The next few problems
will show that f(3, 5) = 1/4.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
8. Since there are ten pieces of muﬃn to be apportioned amongst three students, at
least one of the students must receive at least four pieces (this is one version of the
pigeonhole principle). If a student receives four pieces of muﬃn totaling 5/3 of a muﬃn,
the smallest of those pieces cannot be larger than 5/3
4 = 5/12. Thus 5/12 is the largest
that the smallest piece anyone receives could be.

criteria.name: Problem 10
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 2 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 2. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
10. If someone gets a single piece of size 3/5, explain why someone else must get a piece
that is smaller than 1/4. (Hint: what happens to the other 2/5 of the muﬃn from
which the 3/5 piece was taken?)
[2 pts.]

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
10. If someone gets their fair 3/5 of a muﬃn in a single piece, then the muﬃn from which
that piece was cut has 2/5 left over. If that piece is also given to a single person, then
that person still needs 1/5 of a muﬃn to obtain their fair share. So all the other pieces
of muﬃn they receive must be at most 1/5 < 1/4 in size. Thus the smallest piece
someone gets would be smaller than 1/4. On the other hand if the 2/5 leftover piece
is cut into two or more pieces, then one of those pieces is at most 1/5 in size, and once
again someone will receive a piece smaller than 1/4. So the best division of 3 muﬃns
among 5 students cannot have someone receiving a single 3/5-sized piece.

1/4, so no one gets three or more pieces.

14. Explain why if there is some muﬃn that is cut into three or more pieces the upper
bound is satisﬁed.

OFFICIAL REFERENCE:
14. If some muﬃn is cut into three or more pieces, than at least one of those pieces must

criteria.name: Problem 18
criteria.description:
Use the official reference below, allowing equivalent valid proofs. Award at most 4 points. Printed subpart maxima in order: 4. Partial credit is a benchmark judgment, not an official detailed marking scheme. PDF layouts and diagrams remain authoritative.

TASK AND LOCAL CONTEXT:
18. For a ﬁnal challenge, prove that f(24, 25) = 8/25.
[4 pts.]
Contest ends here.
3


No contest material on this page.
Much more is known about the function f(m, s). For examples, it is simple to see that
f(km, ks) ≥f(m, s) because any strategy for splitting up m muﬃns among s students
could just be repeated k times to split up km muﬃns for ks students, and the smallest piece
required wouldn’t get any smaller! It is reasonable to think, though, that the extra ﬂexibility
with more muﬃns and more students might allow the smallest piece to increase in size. But
this is not the case! It is not simple to prove, but f(km, ks) = f(m, s).
Together with the fact proven in the contest that f(m, s) = m
s f(s, m) this shows that
f(m, s) can be computed for all values of m and s just by considering those that are relatively
prime and for which m > s. In fact, the problem can be turned into a 1-variable problem by
considering the function g(x) = f(m, s) for x = m/s. This function is very badly behaved,
and doesn’t exhibit much regularity in its graph. Check out the graphs here for some plots
of g(x) over several diﬀerent intervals.
The muﬃn problem is actually a fairly new mathematical puzzle, created in 2010 by a
gentleman named Alan Frank. It was shared in some local puzzle forums for several years
before showing up in a pamphlet of fun problems compiled by Nancy Blachman for the
Julia Robinson Mathematics Festival. Some of these pamphlets found their way to the 2016
Gathering 4 Gardner conference. (Martin Gardner was one of the foremost puzzlesmiths
and mathematical communicators of the 20th century. He wrote the mathematical games
column for Scientiﬁc American for many years before it was taken over by G¨odel, Escher,
Bach author Douglas Hofstadter.) William Gasarch picked up a copy of the pamphlet and
found the problem fun, and had his graduate students start to write programs to solve various
cases.
In 2018, Scott Huddleston wrote a computer program that solves the muﬃn problem
very quickly (linear time complexity!)
but no one had a proof that it worked correctly
in all cases. That would have to wait for 2020 when Richard Chatwin solved an isomor-
phic problem and proved the solution worked.
His paper is available on the arXiv at
arxiv.org/pdf/1907.08726.pdf.
(It is not light reading!).
Gasarch and his students pub-
lished a book about the topic, so if you want to know everything there is to know about the
muﬃn problem, here is a link to the book on Amazon. (ARML receives no consideration for
purchases of this book.)
The problem is recent enough, in fact, that the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences
doesn’t know very much about it! The only sequence in the encyclopedia as of the end of
2023 is sequence A298783 which tells how often the ﬂoor-ceiling upper bound fails to give
the correct answer.
If you’ve enjoyed this contest, treat yourself to some muﬃns! Hopefully you can cut them
so that no one gets only tiny crumbs!

18. This challenge has two parts: ﬁnd a procedure to divide 24 muﬃns among 25 students
so that no one gets a pieces smaller than 8/25, and show that no procedure can produce
a larger smallest piece.
The division procedure ﬁrst. Take six muﬃns and divide them into 12/25- and 13/25-
sized pieces. The next six will be divided into 11/25- and 14/25-sized pieces. The next
six into 10/25- and 15/25-sized pieces. The last six muﬃns are divided into two pieces
of size 8/25 and one of size 9/25.
Take the six 12/25-sized pieces, and give two pieces each to three students, so those
three students now have 24/25 of a muﬃn. The six 13/25- and the six 11/25-sized
pieces can be paired and given to the next six students. The 14/25- and 10/24-sized
pieces go to the next six students, and six more students get one of the 15/25- and one
4


of the 9/25-sized pieces. That leaves 12 pieces of size 8/25; give three of those pieces
to each of the four remaining students and the division has been accomplished.
Now, assume there exists a division of the muﬃns for which the smallest piece anyone
gets is larger than 8/25. First note that no muﬃn can be left uncut, as that would give
someone a whole muﬃn and 1 > 24/25 which is the fair share. On the other hand, no
muﬃn should be cut into four or more pieces, as then one of those would be at most
1/4 < 8/25 in size. So all muﬃns should be cut into either two or three pieces.
Among the students, no one can get just one piece, because that piece would have to
be of size 24/25 and the remaining pieces of that muﬃn are all less than 8/25 in size.
On the other hand, if some student gets three or more pieces, then one of them is at
most 24/25

= 8/25 and the assumption is that the smallest piece anyone receives is
larger than that. Thus, each of the 25 students receives exactly two pieces of muﬃn.
That means there are 50 total pieces of muﬃn. Since each muﬃn is cut into either two
or three pieces, to obtain 50 pieces requires that 22 muﬃns are cut into two pieces and
2 are cut into three pieces.
For the two muﬃns that are cut into three pieces, those pieces are all strictly between
8/25 and 9/25 in size. Larger than 8/25 by assumption, and smaller than 9/25 because
if one piece is at least 9/25 then the other two pieces of that muﬃn total at most 16/25
so one of them is at most 8/25. Furthermore, none of the muﬃns that are cut into
only two pieces can have one of those pieces in this range, because then the other piece
of that muﬃn must be at least 16/25 in size, and for the student who has that piece,
their other piece will be less than 8/25. So there are exactly six pieces of muﬃn whose
size is strictly between 8/25 and 9/25.
Now consider the students who own those six pieces. Their other piece—recall that
each student has exactly two pieces of muﬃn—will be strictly between 15/25 and 16/25.
Furthermore, there can be no other pieces of muﬃn in this range because if there are,
then for the student who owns such a piece, their other piece would be between 8/25
and 9/25 and those pieces are already all accounted for. So there are exactly six muﬃn
pieces between 15/25 and 16/25.
Next, for each of those pieces, consider the other piece of the muﬃn from which it
came (note that all the muﬃns that have been cut into three pieces have already been
considered). Those pieces must all be strictly between 9/25 and 10/25 in size. Again,
there cannot be any other pieces of muﬃns in that range, because the other piece of
the muﬃn from which they come would be between 15/25 and 16/25 and again, those
are already accounted for. So there are exactly six pieces of muﬃn with size between
9/25 and 10/25.
Continue in this fashion. Consider the students who own those pieces. Their other
pieces are all strictly between 14/25 and 15/25 in size. Keep going back and forth
between the two pieces owned by a student and the two pieces into which the muﬃns
are split. The conclusion is that there are exactly six pieces of muﬃn of size in each of
the intervals (8/25, 9/25), (9/25, 10/25), (10/25, 11/25), . . . , (15/25, 16/25). There are
eight such intervals, each containing six pieces of muﬃn, totalling 48 pieces of muﬃn.

Since there must be 50 pieces of muﬃn, a contradiction has been reached, showing that
there is no division of 24 muﬃns among 25 students where the smallest piece anyone
gets is more than 8/25.
